To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

decreasing output prices, increasing direct subsidies and large land area increase the probability of switching from standard to organic farming, and that intensive livestock production, labour intensive production and low yields decrease the probability of the switch.
the switch to organic technology is more likely on farms that are more intensive in terms of labour input, have larger land areas, and are less intensive in terms of livestock production and yield.
The results suggest that increasing direct subsidies and decreasing output prices trigger the switch to an organic farm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether organic farming is an economically viable alternative to standard farming.
the question of whether and to what extent the choice between standard farming and organic farming can be influenced by policies.
the question how farmers react to the introduction of policies promoting organic farming technologies in the context of the EU.

organic farming is more likely on larger, less intensive farms with low yields and low labour inputs.

the switch is most likely on farms with high land areas and low output prices.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the switch to organic agriculture is not a one-way street, as the results suggest that the probability of switching back to standard farming increases when direct subsidies decrease.
the choice between standard farming and organic farming is a dynamic decision.

the choice of farming technology is not a one-time decision, but rather an intertemporal choice that is affected by future expected revenues, which are in turn determined by the future expected prices of agricultural commodities.
